issues.legal_issue: Payments made in consideration of transferred monopoly rights and a licence are capital expenditure rather than deductible business expenditure.
material_facts: The company obtained transferred monopoly and licence rights under an agreement with the original grantee and his nominee.
Under the agreement, the company was to make annual payments to the transferor and his nominee based on the business's net profits while the monopoly rights and licence continued.
The company claimed deductions for those payments, but did not press that claim before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The payments for the monopoly rights were capital in nature and were not deductible as business expenditure.
issues.legal_principle: The Court's final answer characterized the monopoly-rights payments as capital expenditure. The claim was not pressed, and the judgment gives no further analysis of this issue. The deduction question arose under sections 10(1) and 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.

predicates.income_tax_deduction_appeal: The matter is an income-tax appeal concerning a claim to deduct a business payment.
predicates.payment_made_for_transferred_monopoly_ri: The taxpayer made a payment under an arrangement in consideration of transferred monopoly rights and a licence.

issues.definition: When an income-tax deduction appeal concerns a payment made for transferred monopoly rights, that payment is treated as capital expenditure.

issues.legal_issue: A royalty calculated directly by reference to manufactured goods is revenue expenditure when it is not paid to secure an enduring advantage.
material_facts: The grant required payment of a royalty calculated as a percentage of the price of sugar manufactured, and allowed the rate to be reconsidered if it was found excessive after five years.
The grant stated that no other tax would be charged on the sugar manufactured.
The Court found that the royalty payment was directly related to the sugar manufactured and was not a payment for securing an enduring advantage or for the monopoly rights.
The company claimed deductions for the royalty paid on sugar, and the dispute before the Supreme Court concerned whether that royalty was capital or revenue expenditure.
issues.conclusion: The royalty paid on sugar was revenue expenditure deductible under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Whether expenditure is capital or revenue depends on the facts, including the nature of the trade, the character and purpose of the payment, and the asset or advantage for which it is made; no single test is exhaustive or universal. A royalty directly related to output or raw material obtained, rather than paid to acquire an enduring advantage, is revenue expenditure. The Court applied section 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, followed Gotan Lime Syndicate v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Associated Stone Industries (Kotah) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, referred to Singareni Collieries Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and R. B. Seth Moolchand Suganchand v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and explained that Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax concerned a payment for acquiring an enduring asset or advantage.

predicates.royalty_calculated_by_reference_to_outpu: The taxpayer paid a royalty calculated directly by reference to goods manufactured or raw material obtained in carrying on the business.
predicates.payment_not_for_enduring_advantage: The royalty was not paid to acquire an enduring advantage or asset.

issues.definition: When an income-tax deduction appeal concerns a royalty calculated by reference to output and not paid to acquire an enduring advantage, the royalty is treated as revenue expenditure.
